terminal.description: A shell in your workspace: node run.mjs <file> runs a file against a fresh copy of the bakehouse database, so changes are never saved.

tasks.title: Sign up a new cafe
tasks.description:
A new cafe has signed up and placed its first order on the same day.

In `queries/1-new-cafe.sql`, write two `INSERT` statements:

1. Add a cafe named `The Lantern Room` in the town `Wyndham Cross`, with contact email `hello@lanternroom.example`, joined on `2026-11-19`.
2. Add an order for that cafe, ordered on `2026-11-19`, with status `pending` and no driver (`NULL`).

Do not type any ids. Let the database choose the new ids, and look up the new cafe's id with a subquery by its name.

The check runs your file and compares the whole `cafes` and `orders` tables with the expected tables, on the shipped data and on a hidden dataset with a different number of cafes and orders.
nextSteps: Insert the cafe, listing the columns you fill in.
Add `SELECT * FROM cafes;` at the end of the file and run it to see the new row.
Insert the order, finding the cafe id with a subquery.
Check the new order points at the new cafe, then remove the extra SELECT if you like.
hints: Leave id out of the column list and SQLite gives an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY column the next free number.
A value in VALUES can be a subquery in parentheses, as long as it returns one value.
For the order, put (SELECT id FROM cafes WHERE name = 'The Lantern Room') where the cafe_id value goes, and write NULL for driver_id.

tasks.title: Apply the price review
tasks.description:
Flour went up, and Tobias has two changes for the product list. In `queries/2-price-review.sql`:

1. `UPDATE`: raise the price of every product in the `bread` category by 5%, rounded to 2 decimals with `ROUND(..., 2)`. No other product changes.
2. `DELETE`: remove products that are out of stock (`stock` is 0) **and** have never been ordered (they appear in no `order_items` row). Products that are out of stock but appear in past orders must stay, or old orders would point at nothing.

The check runs your file and compares the whole `products` table with the expected table, on the shipped data and on a hidden dataset.
nextSteps: Write each WHERE clause as a SELECT first and check which rows it finds.
Turn the first SELECT into the UPDATE and run it with a SELECT after it.
Turn the second SELECT into the DELETE.
Check that out-of-stock products with past orders are still there.
hints: An UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause changes every row in the table.
SET can use the old value of the column: price = price * 1.05 reads the current price of each row.
The delete needs both conditions: stock = 0 AND the id is NOT IN the list of product ids from order_items.

tasks.title: Cancel an order in one transaction
tasks.description:
The cafe behind order `27` has closed for repairs, and the order must be cancelled. Its items were set aside from stock when it was placed, so they go back on the shelf.

In `queries/3-cancel-order.sql`, inside one transaction (`BEGIN;` ... `COMMIT;`):

1. Add the `quantity` of each item in order 27 back to that product's `stock`. Other products do not change.
2. Set the status of order 27 to `cancelled`.

Keep the order's rows in `order_items`. Do not type the product ids or quantities: read them from `order_items`, because the hidden dataset has different items in order 27.

The check compares the `products`, `orders` and `order_items` tables with the expected tables on both datasets, checks that your file opens and commits a transaction, and checks that the total stock went up by exactly the number of items in the order.
nextSteps: SELECT the items of order 27 and the current stock of those products.
Write the stock UPDATE with a subquery and check the new stock values.
Wrap both in BEGIN and COMMIT and run the file.
hints: The new stock of a product depends on its own row in order_items, so the UPDATE needs a correlated subquery.
Inside SET, (SELECT quantity FROM order_items WHERE order_id = 27 AND product_id = products.id) is the amount for the row being updated.
Without a WHERE on the UPDATE, products not in the order get NULL from the subquery, and SQLite refuses to store a NULL stock. Limit the UPDATE to ids IN the order's product ids.
